description: We are a close-knit group of 4 innovators focused on building a creative, high-impact solution using satellite and space agency data. Our primary goal for this hackathon is to collaborate effectively, learn new technical tools, and deliver a high-quality prototype and pitch presentation by the deadline.
summary:
ECHO: Satellite imagery. Brought into 3D.

ECHO is an interactive 3D web explorer that helps students, educators and curious non-specialists understand what NASA-ISRO NISAR radar sees changing on Earth. We drape real Sentinel-2 colour imagery over Copernicus GLO-30 terrain and add dated NISAR observations. Users orbit a real landscape, play and rewind short event stories, move a divider between dates, and open the evidence, dates and limits behind each result.

ECHO includes seven events: floods in India, the Plaskett wildfire, lava growth at Krasheninnikov volcano, Hubbard Glacier, the La Guaira earthquake, Rota island and forest clearing in Brazil. Our slides feature Plaskett, where HV radar return fell 4.30 dB over a burn scar confirmed by optical imagery and the fire perimeter. Our video shows the same method on the volcano.

Each event keeps its own dates, units and caveats. These are selected examples, not damage maps, and some radar data is provisional.

It matters because NISAR will produce enormous amounts of free data, and its value depends on people being able to interpret it. ECHO turns radar numbers into a place people recognise, for communities, educators and decision-makers.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

ECHO (Earth Replay) is an interactive 3D web explorer that helps people understand surface change seen by NASA-ISRO NISAR radar. We drape real Sentinel-2 colour imagery over Copernicus GLO-30 terrain and add dated NISAR observations as before/after comparisons.

Users choose an event, play, pause and rewind a short illustrated story, move a divider between dates, and open an evidence panel showing observation dates, values, layers and sources.

ECHO includes seven events: Gandak floods (India), Plaskett wildfire (USA), Krasheninnikov lava growth (Russia), Hubbard Glacier (Canada), La Guaira earthquake (Venezuela), Rota (Northern Mariana Islands) and Altamira forest clearing (Brazil). Our slides feature Plaskett, where NISAR HV radar return fell 4.30 dB over a burn scar supported by optical imagery and the NIFC fire perimeter. Our video shows the same method on the volcano.

Behind the app, Python scripts turn NISAR GCOV backscatter from ASF DAAC into web-ready textures and data. The browser loads these prepared files, so viewers need no login and no live satellite backend.

What benefits does it have?

ECHO turns radar numbers into a place people recognise. Learners see what changed, when it changed, and how sure we are. Every event keeps its own dates, units and caveats, and the evidence is always one click away. The app is free to use, needs no account, and runs in a browser.

What is the intended impact?

NISAR will produce large amounts of free data, and its value depends on people being able to interpret it. ECHO aims to help students, educators and curious non-specialists build that understanding. It is an educational prototype. We have not measured learning outcomes and make no claims about them.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

App: React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei, MapLibre GL JS

Data preparation: Python with rasterio, NumPy, h5py, SciPy, pyproj and earthaccess

Hosting and source: Vercel, and a public GitHub repository (MIT licence for app code)

Data: NISAR GCOV (ASF DAAC), NASA/Caltech NISAR-derived Venezuela product, Copernicus Sentinel-2, Copernicus GLO-30, NIFC WFIGS, INPE DETER

Hardware: none special. The app runs in a standard web browser.

AI disclosure: OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex contributed substantially to research, concept refinement, code, data processing, design, validation, documentation and deployment. Tenrai (Gaurav Ranade) directed the product, selected the events and reviewed each iteration. The app contains no trained machine-learning model. The video uses ElevenLabs narration.

How is your project creative?

Most radar tools show maps and charts. ECHO tells each change as a short story on real terrain, with a before/after divider, illustrated process animations that explain possible causes, and evidence on demand. We use real satellite imagery rather than generated pictures, which keeps every scene grounded in a place that actually exists.

What factors did your team consider?

Honesty: blue and red describe radar backscatter, not damage. Values are selected examples, not representative surveys, and some radar data is provisional with unresolved QA checks.

Audience: plain-language explanations for non-specialists, with India as the default event.

Dates: optical and radar acquisition dates differ, and we label both.

Method: Venezuela uses a separate relative-motion legend and is never read as backscatter.

Licences and privacy: provider terms are kept, no accounts or analytics are used, and no agency endorsement is claimed.

Limits: process animations are illustrative, relief is exaggerated for display, and ECHO is not an operational hazard tool.
